title: How can embedding models bind concepts?
claim: Scenes are built from objects that are tuples of concepts, and recognizing concepts is a different test from recognizing objects.
layout: 3 panels: top-left and top-right spaces, bottom two score tables, with tree
description: Figure with three labeled panels. Panel (a), top left, shows a 3x3 grid for the concept space C. Rows are colors (green, red, blue), columns are shapes (triangle, square, circle), and each cell holds a colored shape. Panel (b), top right, shows the scene space S as a set of small boxes, each holding two colored shapes. Below it, a tree splits one scene s = (o1, o2) into o1 = (red, square) and o2 = (blue, circle), shown in rounded boxes. Panel (c), along the bottom, has two tables. Concept recognition lists present concepts (red, blue, square, circle) with similarity 1.0 and absent concepts (triangle ... green) with 0.0. Object recognition lists present objects (blue circle, red square) with 1.0 and absent combinations (red circle ... blue square) with 0.0. A red square and a blue circle in a box serve as the example input x. Red, green and blue colors carry through every panel.
caption: Schematic of the binding setup. (a) Example concept space C (e.g., color × shape), where each object is a tuple of concept values. (b) Example scene space S, where a scene s is a tuple of objects (here, two objects (o1, o2)). (c) Example of the two recognition criteria: concept recognition ranks present concept values above absent ones (Def. 3.3), while object recognition ranks present objects above absent concept combinations (Def. 3.4).
abstract: Humans easily determine which color belongs to which shape in multi-object scenes, an ability known as concept binding. Vision-language embedding models such as CLIP struggle with binding: they recognize individual concepts but fail to represent which concepts form which objects. Although CLIP behaves like a bag-of-concepts model in cross-modal retrieval, object information is recoverable from its image and text embeddings separately. We study this tension through the binding function, which maps concepts to scene embeddings. We find that scene embeddings decompose additively into object representations, explaining why uni-modal probes can recover object information. However, CLIP's binding function is high-complexity, which likely prevents the image and text encoders from learning a shared binding mechanism that generalizes to unseen concept combinations. We then ask whether this limitation is fundamental. We show that it is not. In controlled transformer models trained from scratch, binding generalization emerges with sufficient data coverage. These models learn low-complexity binding functions characterized by multiplicative interactions between concepts, enabling systematic generalization. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/oshapio/binding-concepts-complexity.
